Hyundai has big plans for[its performance-oriented N division](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2025-hyundai-ioniq-5-n-review-surprise-delight-recharge/) . Speaking during the South Korean company’s annual Investor Day, CEO José Muñoz announced that new, volume-focused Hyundai N models are on their way to help the division reach its goal of selling 100,000 cars annually by 2030. These include a rear-wheel-drive model and cars positioned between N and N Line models. Crossing the 100,000-unit threshold represents an ambitious bet for Hyundai N; Its annual sales totaled about 20,000 cars in 2025.


N is counting on several new models to grow quickly in a relatively short amount of time. These include an entry-level SUV that will be based on a front-wheel-drive platform and a yet-unnamed new model built on a rear-wheel-drive architecture, though all-wheel-drive will be available. Specific details haven’t been shared yet, so we don’t know whether the rear-wheel-drive model will land as a coupe, a crossover, or a sedan. Similarly, there’s no word yet on whether it will be electrified, and how. However, an earlier report[claims](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/hyundai-n-vision-74-is-go-for-launch-report/) that the hydrogen-powered, retro-inspired N Vision 74 Coupe (pictured) will soon spawn a production car. Could this be it?


Hyundai N is not counting N Line models in its annual sales, which is a wise move as these are essentially regular-production cars with an appearance package. Not all of its upcoming cars will be full-blown N models, though. Looking ahead, the brand will launch a range of cars that it describes as “high-volume performance.” These will be positioned between N and N Line, and they will share their drivetrain and other parts with N cars, but they’ll be tuned for daily driving rather than to post the quickest possible lap times. They’ll be more affordable, too, so they’ll play a significant role in helping N reach its sales goals over the next few years.

# What’s Next for Hyundai?


Zooming out beyond the N division, Hyundai will launch over 100 new and refreshed vehicles globally by the end of the decade in a bid to sell 5.55 million cars annually in 2030. North America will receive 58 of those, including models that are pegged in what the company calls “white spaces,” meaning segments in which it’s either underrepresented or not present. Interestingly, Hyundai highlighted body-on-frame vehicles, and notably a mid-size pickup, as a market segment with a significant opportunity for growth.


We’ve heard numerous rumors over the past few years detailing a Hyundai off-roader designed for North America. The outdoorsy[Boulder concept](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/hyundai-boulder-concept-pictures/) (pictured below), introduced in April 2026, looks like a[Wrangler](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/review-2022-jeep-wrangler-rubicon-392/) competitor, but it was actually developed to preview a body-on-frame pickup due out by 2030. Details remain few and far between, but the Boulder connection suggests that Hyundai’s pickup will put a bigger focus on adventure than on towing capability. It could share some of its underpinnings with[the Kia Tasman](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2025-kia-tasman-specs-pictures-features/) sold in overseas markets, though it will likely need to be built in the United States to circumvent[the Chicken Tax](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/so-what-is-the-chicken-tax-anyway/) .
